title: Inversion, Cleft Sentences and Emphasis
summary: Subject-auxiliary inversion after fronted negatives, inverted conditionals, it- and wh-clefts, and the register all of them belong to.

sections.heading: Fronted Negatives and Subject-Auxiliary Inversion
sections.body:
When a **negative or restrictive adverbial** is moved to the front of a clause for emphasis, the subject and the first auxiliary change places. The word order becomes identical to that of a question.

The adverbials that trigger this include `never`, `rarely`, `seldom`, `hardly`, `scarcely`, `no sooner`, `not only`, `not until`, `at no time`, `under no circumstances`, `on no account`, `little` in the sense of `not at all`, and `only` with a following adverbial such as `only after`, `only when`, `only then` or `only if`.

Nothing about the meaning changes. The inversion is the price of the fronting, and it is obligatory once the fronting has happened.

examples.right: Never had she seen results so consistent.
examples.wrong: Never she had seen results so consistent.
examples.note: The fronted negative pulls the auxiliary in front of the subject.

examples.right: Under no circumstances should the samples be left unrefrigerated.
examples.wrong: Under no circumstances the samples should be left unrefrigerated.
examples.note: A negative prepositional phrase triggers the same inversion.

examples.right: Little did he know that the data had already been withdrawn.
examples.note: `Little` here means `not at all` and counts as a negative adverbial.

examples.right: She had never seen results so consistent.
examples.note: In ordinary word order there is no inversion at all; only the fronting causes it.

sections.heading: Simple Tenses: Where do, does and did Come From
sections.body:
Inversion moves an auxiliary. If the clause is in the present simple or past simple, there is no auxiliary to move, so English supplies one: `do`, `does` or `did`.

This is exactly the mechanism of ordinary questions, and it has the same consequence. Once `do` carries the tense, the main verb returns to its **bare infinitive** form: `did the government publish`, not `did the government published`.

English never inverts a lexical verb. `Rarely occurs this species` is not an option in modern English, however natural verb-subject order may feel from another language.

examples.right: Rarely does this species occur below 2,000 metres.
examples.wrong: Rarely occurs this species below 2,000 metres.
examples.note: The main verb cannot invert; `does` is inserted and `occur` returns to the bare form.

examples.right: Not until 1998 did the government publish the full figures.
examples.wrong: Not until 1998 the government published the full figures.
examples.note: The fronted negative requires do-support even though the sentence is otherwise complete.

examples.right: Seldom do students revise the entire syllabus.
examples.wrong: Seldom students revise the entire syllabus.
examples.note: Present simple with a plural subject takes `do`.

sections.heading: Not only, No sooner, Hardly and Only
sections.body:
Several of these patterns come in two halves, and the halves are fixed. `Not only` pairs with `but ... also`; `no sooner` pairs with `than`; `hardly` and `scarcely` pair with `when` or `before`.

In every two-part pattern the inversion falls on the **first** clause only. The second clause has ordinary word order.

With `only when`, `only after` and `only if`, there is one further trap. The fronted element is the whole subordinate clause, so the inversion appears in the **main** clause that follows it, not inside the subordinate clause itself.

examples.right: Not only did the costs rise, but the timetable also slipped.
examples.wrong: Not only the costs rose, but also the timetable slipped.
examples.note: Inversion applies to the first clause; the second keeps normal order.

examples.right: No sooner had the results appeared than the criticism began.
examples.wrong: No sooner had the results appeared when the criticism began.
examples.note: `no sooner` is completed by `than`, never by `when`.

examples.right: Hardly had the session begun when the power failed.
examples.wrong: Hardly had the session begun than the power failed.
examples.note: `hardly` and `scarcely` take `when` or `before`; only `no sooner` takes `than`.

examples.right: Only after the audit was completed did the board approve the budget.
examples.wrong: Only after the audit was completed the board approved the budget.
examples.note: The inversion belongs to the main clause, not to the `only after` clause.

sections.heading: Inversion in Conditionals
sections.body:
Formal English can drop `if` and invert instead. Three patterns exist: `Had we known` for the past unreal, `Were it not for` or `Were she to accept` for the present unreal, and `Should you require` for a real but tentative future condition.

Only `had`, `were` and `should` can be fronted this way. `Were` is used for all persons in this construction, since it is the subjunctive form.

The negative cannot be contracted. `Had we not known` is correct; `Hadn't we known` reads as a question and is not available here.

examples.right: Had we known the risks, we would have postponed the trial.
examples.note: Equivalent to `If we had known`; `if` disappears and `had` moves to the front.

examples.right: Should you require further information, please contact the registrar.
examples.note: This replaces `If you should require` and is standard in formal correspondence.

examples.right: Were it not for the grant, the department would have closed.
examples.wrong: Was it not for the grant, the department would have closed.
examples.note: The construction uses the subjunctive `were` regardless of the subject.

examples.right: Had the committee not intervened, the funding would have lapsed.
examples.wrong: Hadn't the committee intervened, the funding would have lapsed.
examples.note: The contracted negative is impossible in an inverted conditional.

sections.heading: It-Clefts and Wh-Clefts
sections.body:
A **cleft** sentence splits one clause into two in order to place a spotlight on a single element.

The **it-cleft** has the shape `It + be + focus + that`. The focus can be a noun phrase, a person, or an adverbial of time or place, and `that` is used throughout, although `who` is available when the focus is a person. It is particularly useful for correcting a wrong assumption.

The **wh-cleft** has the shape `What ... + be + focus`, and it works the other way round, holding the new information back to the end of the sentence, where English prefers to put it.

examples.right: It was the funding that failed, not the research design.
examples.note: The it-cleft isolates `the funding` as the single element in focus.

examples.right: It was in 2011 that the policy was first tested.
examples.note: An adverbial can be the focus, and `that` is used even for time and place.

examples.right: What surprised us was the cost.
examples.note: The wh-cleft delays the new information to the end of the sentence.

examples.right: It was Dr Nasr who first identified the pattern.
examples.wrong: It was Dr Nasr which first identified the pattern.
examples.note: With a person the link is `who` or `that`; `which` is never possible.

sections.heading: Fronting, Register and Ordinary Questions
sections.body:
Not all fronting causes inversion. An object or a complement can be moved to the front for emphasis while the subject and verb stay in their usual order: `This point I will return to later`. Inversion follows only the negative and restrictive adverbials, and the pattern `So + adjective + be`.

Register matters as much as accuracy here. Fronted inversion belongs to formal writing, public speaking and exam-style discursive prose. In casual conversation it sounds theatrical, and one instance in an essay is persuasive where four in a row are merely mannered.

It is worth noticing that the mechanism is not exotic at all. The word order of `Did the committee approve the budget?` is the same word order as `Not until later did the committee approve the budget`, which is why the do-support and the bare infinitive appear in both.

examples.right: So dense was the fog that all flights were suspended.
examples.note: A fronted `so + adjective` triggers inversion; the effect is emphatic and formal.

examples.right: This point I will return to in the final section.
examples.note: Fronting without inversion: the object moves for emphasis, subject and verb do not.

examples.right: Did the committee approve the budget?
examples.note: The same inversion as in the fronted patterns, which is why `did` appears with the bare `approve`.

examples.right: Never in the field of public health has a programme been scaled so quickly.
examples.note: Appropriate in formal writing or a speech, and out of place in everyday conversation.

slips: Fronting without inverting: `Never I have seen` must be `Never have I seen`.
Inverting the main verb: `Rarely occurs it` is not English; insert do-support instead - `Rarely does it occur`.
Leaving the tense on the main verb: after `did` the verb is bare, so `did the government publish`, not `did the government published`.
`No sooner ... when`: the fixed pair is `no sooner ... than`, while `hardly` and `scarcely` take `when`.
Contracting an inverted conditional: write `Had we not known`, never `Hadn't we known`.
Inverting the wrong clause: `Only when the funding arrived did the work begin` - the main clause inverts, not the `only when` clause.

questions.prompt: Never in the history of the department ___ a proposal been rejected so quickly.
questions.explain: The verb phrase is `had been rejected`, so fronting `never` moves only the first auxiliary in front of the subject. Do-support is used only when no auxiliary is already present.

questions.prompt: Rarely ___ a single study change government policy so quickly.
questions.hint: one word: the auxiliary the fronted adverbial forces, present simple
questions.explain: The present simple has no auxiliary to invert, so `does` is supplied and the main verb stays in its bare form, `change`.

questions.prompt: Only when the funding was confirmed ___ the team begin the fieldwork.
questions.explain: With `only when`, the inversion falls on the main clause, and the past simple requires `did` plus the bare infinitive `begin`.

questions.prompt: ___ had the announcement been made than share prices began to fall.
questions.explain: `than` completes only the `no sooner` pattern. `Hardly` and `scarcely` take `when` or `before`, and `not only` takes `but also`.

questions.prompt: ___ not for the emergency grant, the laboratory would have closed last year.
questions.hint: two words: the inverted form of 'If it were not for'
questions.explain: The inverted conditional drops `if` and fronts the subjunctive `were`, which is used for every subject in this pattern.

questions.prompt: ___ we known about the funding cut, we would have applied a month earlier.
questions.explain: The inverted third conditional fronts `had` and omits `if` altogether; `If` would require the ordinary order `If we had known`.

questions.prompt: ___ surprised the researchers most was the speed of the recovery.
questions.hint: one word: the opening of a wh-cleft
questions.explain: The wh-cleft opens with `what`, meaning `the thing that`, and holds the new information back to the end of the sentence.

questions.prompt: ___ the cost that deterred the applicants, not the complexity of the design.
questions.explain: An it-cleft places the focus between `It was` and `that`. `There was` would assert existence rather than single out one element for correction.

questions.prompt: Under no circumstances ___ removed from the secure laboratory.
questions.explain: The fronted negative phrase inverts the subject and the first auxiliary only; the rest of the verb phrase stays in its normal position.

questions.prompt: Should you ___ further assistance with the application, please contact the admissions office.
questions.explain: This inverted conditional replaces `If you should require`, and the verb after `should` is always a bare infinitive.

questions.prompt: So ___ was the response to the consultation that the organisers extended the deadline.
questions.explain: The fronted pattern is `So + adjective + be`, and `be` needs an adjective as its complement; an adverb cannot fill that slot.

questions.prompt: Hardly had the meeting begun ___ the fire alarm sounded.
questions.hint: one word: the conjunction that completes the 'hardly' pattern
questions.explain: `hardly` and `scarcely` are completed by `when` or `before`; `than` belongs only to the `no sooner` pattern.
